sections.skill: Use a randomized experiment and simulation to test whether an association is causal

questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.skill: Use a randomized experiment and simulation to test whether an association is causal
questions.standard_level: Probability & Statistics. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Probability & Statistics, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: Observational data show r = -0.6 between evening screen time and hours of sleep. To test cause, 50 volunteers were randomly assigned to no screens after 8 p.m. or to their usual habits. The no-screen group slept 0.5 hour more on average. In 1,000 random regroupings, a difference of at least 0.5 hour (no-screen minus usual) happened 2 times. Using a 5% threshold, is the difference significant? Explain.
questions.prompt_markup:
Observational data show r = -0.6 between evening screen time and hours of sleep. To test cause, 50 volunteers were randomly assigned to no screens after 8 p.m. or to their usual habits. The no-screen group slept 0.5 hour more on average. In 1,000 random regroupings, a difference of at least 0.5 hour (no-screen minus usual) happened 2 times.
Using a 5% threshold, is the difference significant? Explain.
questions.correct_answer: Yes. 2 ÷ 1,000 = 0.2%, which is below 5%, so chance alone is very unlikely to explain it; cutting evening screens likely increased sleep for volunteers like these.
questions.grading_note: Form required: the decision with the simulated proportion compared with 5%.

questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.skill: Use a randomized experiment and simulation to test whether an association is causal
questions.standard_level: Probability & Statistics. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Probability & Statistics, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: Why can this randomized experiment, but not the observational correlation alone, support the claim that evening screens reduce sleep?
questions.prompt_markup: Why can this randomized experiment, but not the observational correlation alone, support the claim that evening screens reduce sleep?
questions.correct_answer: Random assignment tends to balance other variables (such as stress or age) between the groups, so a significant difference can be credited to the treatment; in observational data a lurking variable could explain the correlation.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent explanation that contrasts random assignment with possible lurking variables.

questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.skill: Use a randomized experiment and simulation to test whether an association is causal
questions.standard_level: Probability & Statistics. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Probability & Statistics, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: In a randomization test, the observed difference was matched or exceeded in 350 of 1,000 regroupings. Using a 5% threshold, what is the conclusion?
questions.prompt_markup:
In a randomization test, the observed difference was matched or exceeded in 350 of 1,000 regroupings.
Using a 5% threshold, what is the conclusion?

choices.text: The treatment definitely has no effect.
The difference is not significant; chance could easily explain it.

questions.correct_answer: The difference is not significant; chance could easily explain it.
questions.grading_note: 350 ÷ 1,000 = 35%, far above 5%. A non-significant result does not prove there is no effect.

questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions

questions.standard_level: Probability & Statistics. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Probability & Statistics, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: A news story says, "r = 0.6, so 60% of the change in sales is caused by advertising." Name two errors.
questions.prompt_markup:
A news story says, "r = 0.6, so 60% of the change in sales is caused by advertising."
Name two errors.
questions.correct_answer: r is not a percent of change (r² ≈ 0.36 describes the share of variation explained), and correlation does not show causation.
questions.grading_note: Form required: two errors.
